summary: The ʿumra is the lesser or minor pilgrimage to Mecca, performable at any time of year, in contrast to the hajj, which is tied to appointed days. The Qur'an commands, 'And complete the hajj and ʿumra for Allah' (Q 2:196), and a canonical hadith reports that one ʿumra to the next is an expiation for what lies between them (Sahih al-Bukhari 1773). Its rites in the tradition's account are ihram (consecration), tawaf (circumambulation of the Kaʿba), saʿy (the going between Safa and Marwa), and halq or taqsir (shaving or shortening the hair). Whether the ʿumra is obligatory once in a lifetime or a recommended sunna is a recorded disagreement among the legal schools, attributed here and not adjudicated.
description:
The ʿumra (from the root ʿ-m-r; the term is often glossed as a visitation) is the lesser pilgrimage to Mecca. Unlike the hajj, whose essential rites are bound to the appointed days of Dhu al-Hijja, the ʿumra may in the tradition's account be performed at any time of the year, and it omits the rites specific to the hajj (the standing at ʿArafat, Muzdalifa, and the rites at Mina). The Qur'anic anchor names both pilgrimages together: Q 2:196 commands, in the Saheeh International rendering, 'And complete the hajj and ʿumra for Allah' (wa-atimmu al-hajja wa-l-ʿumrata lillah), and the verse continues with provisions for the pilgrim who is prevented from completing the rites.

The rites of the ʿumra are described here as the tradition's attributed practice. The pilgrim enters ihram, the consecrated state, at the appointed boundary (miqat), putting on (for men) two seamless white cloths, pronouncing the talbiya, and abstaining from certain ordinary acts; performs the tawaf, the sevenfold circumambulation of the Kaʿba; performs the saʿy, the going seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa; and concludes with halq or taqsir, the shaving or shortening of the hair, by which the pilgrim leaves the state of ihram. The schools also treat the ways the ʿumra may be joined with the hajj in a single journey (in the classifications commonly called tamattuʿ, qiran, and ifrad), and their detailed rules differ; the details are left to the schools and not ruled on here.

The merit of the ʿumra is carried in the canonical Sunna. Sahih al-Bukhari reports on the authority of Abu Huraira that the Prophet said, '(The performance of) ʿUmra is an expiation for the sins committed (between it and the previous one). And the reward of Hajj Mabrur (the one accepted by Allah) is nothing except Paradise' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1773, the opening hadith of the Book of ʿUmra); Bukhari's own Arabic chapter heading there reads bab wujub al-ʿumra wa-fadliha (the chapter on the obligation of the ʿumra and its merit).

Whether the ʿumra is obligatory is a recorded disagreement among the legal schools, and it is reported here as their attributed positions. In the account transmitted in the comparative-law literature, notably Ibn Rushd's Bidayat al-Mujtahid, the Shafiʿi and Hanbali schools hold the ʿumra to be obligatory (wajib) once in a lifetime on those able, while the Hanafi and Maliki schools hold it to be a recommended sunna rather than an obligation; each side invokes its own textual proofs. None of these positions is ranked or resolved here; the disagreement itself is a standing example of the schools' recorded diversity. This entry describes the ʿumra on the tradition's own terms and reports its rites, merits, and disputed status as that tradition's account, without adjudicating them.

relations.note: The ʿumra (lesser pilgrimage) is distinguished from the hajj (greater pilgrimage): the ʿumra may be performed at any time of year and omits the rites specific to the hajj, while the hajj is tied to the appointed days; Q 2:196 commands the completion of both for God. Mirror of the related_to edge in the hajj entry.

Whether the ʿumra is obligatory once in a lifetime (the position attributed to the Shafiʿi and Hanbali schools) or a recommended sunna (the position attributed to the Hanafi and Maliki schools) is a recorded disagreement among the legal schools (madhhabs); the positions are attributed and not ranked.

historical_period.note: The Qur'anic verse naming the ʿumra (Q 2:196) belongs to the period of the Prophet's mission (c. 610-632 CE); the tradition traces the rites to the Prophet's practice, including the ʿumras he is reported to have performed. The ʿumra remains a living, year-round practice; no end date is asserted.
